title: AVD Architecture and Planning: Control Plane, Host Pools, and App Groups
monthTitle: Azure Virtual Desktop Infrastructure: Plan, Deploy & Scale
summary: This lesson builds the architectural mental model for everything else in this module. You'll learn exactly what Microsoft manages versus what you manage in Azure Virtual Desktop, why reverse connect means you never open an inbound port to a session host, and how host pools, application groups, and workspaces fit together to publish desktops and apps to users. You'll also learn the personal-vs-pooled decision, validation vs production host pools, and the practical service limits that shape how you design at scale — the foundation for AZ-140 Domain 1.
objectives: Draw the line between the Microsoft-managed AVD control plane and the customer-managed session host layer
Explain reverse connect and why AVD requires no inbound firewall ports to session hosts
Differentiate personal and pooled host pools and choose the correct load-balancing algorithm for a pooled pool
Explain how host pools, application groups (Desktop vs RemoteApp), and workspaces relate and how they publish resources to users
Justify when to use a validation host pool versus a production host pool
Identify the practical service limits and planning constraints that shape host pool design at scale

quiz.q: Which statement correctly describes the Azure Virtual Desktop control plane?
options: The customer deploys and patches the broker, web, and gateway services in their own subscription
The control plane and session hosts are both fully managed by Microsoft with no customer configuration
Microsoft hosts and manages the broker, web, and gateway/diagnostics services; the customer owns the session host VMs and the resources they access
The control plane runs inside the customer's virtual network alongside the session hosts
quiz.why: AVD is a managed service: Microsoft operates the connection broker, web access/feed, gateway, and diagnostics components at global scale. The customer's responsibility is the session host VMs (compute, OS, image, network) and everything those VMs can reach — that split is the first thing to internalize about AVD architecture.

quiz.q: Why doesn't Azure Virtual Desktop require an inbound firewall rule or a public IP on the session host VM for users to connect?
options: Because session hosts only accept connections from the same virtual network
Because RDP traffic is tunneled through Microsoft Entra ID by default
Because Azure Bastion is automatically deployed with every host pool
Because the AVD agent on the session host establishes an outbound, persistent connection ('reverse connect') to the AVD service, which then relays the user's session over that channel
quiz.why: The AVD agent on each session host initiates an outbound connection to the Azure Virtual Desktop service (reverse connect). User sessions are relayed over that already-established outbound channel, so you never need an inbound port open, a public IP, or a VPN just to allow users to reach the host — you only need outbound access to the required AVD endpoints.

quiz.q: A pooled host pool needs to keep placing new sessions on the least-loaded host until the pool is close to full, then even it out over time. Which load-balancing algorithm fits, and which host pool type does NOT use load balancing at all?
options: Breadth-first fits the requirement; personal host pools don't use load balancing because each user has a dedicated, assigned host
Depth-first fits the requirement; pooled host pools don't use load balancing
Breadth-first fits the requirement; pooled host pools don't use load balancing
Depth-first fits the requirement; personal host pools use breadth-first by default
quiz.why: Breadth-first spreads new sessions evenly across all available session hosts, maximizing performance per user — the description in the question. Depth-first instead fills one host to its session limit before moving to the next, which is better for cost-driven consolidation. Personal host pools assign each user a specific, dedicated VM, so there's no pool of interchangeable hosts to balance across.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between an application group and a host pool in Azure Virtual Desktop?
options: An application group can span multiple host pools to aggregate resources for a single user base
An application group is a logical grouping of desktops or apps published from the session hosts of exactly one host pool, and it cannot exist without that host pool
An application group replaces the need for a workspace
An application group defines the VNet and subnet the session hosts use
quiz.why: Every application group (Desktop or RemoteApp type) is tied to a single host pool and publishes resources from that pool's session hosts. Workspaces sit a layer above and aggregate one or more application groups so users see a single feed; a host pool with no application group publishes nothing to users.

quiz.q: Why would you deploy a small validation host pool alongside your production host pools?
options: Validation host pools are required by Microsoft licensing before any production pool can be created
Validation host pools automatically mirror production pool capacity for disaster recovery
A validation pool lets you receive new AVD service updates and agent changes early, on a small blast radius, before they roll out broadly to production so you can catch regressions
Validation host pools are the only pool type that supports RemoteApp publishing
quiz.why: Marking a host pool as a validation environment opts it into early exposure to AVD service-side changes and agent updates. Running a small validation pool with a subset of test users lets you catch a regression before it reaches your production fleet — the same 'canary ring' idea used across Azure services.

quiz.q: In two to four sentences, explain what the Azure portal's practical create-flow cap of 500 session hosts per host pool means for planning a 3,000-user pooled deployment, and describe one way an engineer works around it.
quiz.answer: The Azure portal's host pool creation wizard caps how many session hosts you can add in a single create operation at 500, which is a UI/workflow limit rather than a hard architectural ceiling on the host pool resource itself. For a 3,000-user pooled deployment you plan capacity in batches — provisioning and registering session hosts to the same host pool across multiple deployment runs (portal, PowerShell/Az.DesktopVirtualization, or Bicep pipelines), or splitting the user base across multiple host pools with a shared workspace so no single deployment operation has to add more hosts than the tooling supports at once. Either way, the design decision is made at the automation/pipeline level, not by trying to force one enormous single-shot deployment.
quiz.why: Real AVD deployments at scale are always built incrementally — through IaC pipelines that add session hosts in batches or by partitioning users across several host pools — rather than in one operation, and engineers need to plan vCPU quota, availability-set, and deployment-tooling limits alongside the host pool's own configuration.

Preferred application group type behavior for pooled host pools

body_markdown:
## Why This Lesson Exists

AZ-140's biggest domain — planning and implementing an AVD infrastructure — is worth 40 to 45% of the exam, and every task in it assumes you already have the architectural picture in your head. Before you touch a Bicep template or an autoscale plan, you need to know exactly what Microsoft runs for you, what you run yourself, and how the building blocks — host pools, application groups, workspaces — snap together. Get this model right and every later lesson in this module is just filling in detail. Get it wrong and you'll misdiagnose problems for the rest of your AVD career.

## The Control Plane vs. The Session Host Layer

Azure Virtual Desktop is a **managed desktop and app virtualization service** with a hard architectural split:

- **Microsoft-managed control plane**: the connection broker (matches a user to an available session), the web/feed service (what shows up in the client), the gateway (relays session traffic), diagnostics, and the global load-balancing infrastructure. You never patch this, never see a VM for it, and never pay compute for it directly — it's part of the AVD service, available at no additional licensing cost beyond your eligible Windows/Microsoft 365 or per-user access rights.
- **Customer-managed session host layer**: the actual Windows 11 Enterprise multi-session (or single-session) VMs that run in *your* subscription, *your* virtual network, with *your* image, *your* patching cadence, and *your* cost. This is the layer this entire module teaches you to design, deploy, and scale.

This split matters practically: when a user can't log in, the first triage question is always "is this a control-plane problem (feed, broker, auth) or a session-host problem (VM unreachable, agent unhealthy, image broken)?" You'll build that triage skill fully in Module 6, but the architecture split is where it starts.

## Reverse Connect: No Inbound Ports, Ever

A question every AVD newcomer asks: "what inbound NSG rule do I need so users can RDP into my session hosts?" The answer is **none**. AVD uses **reverse connect**: the AVD agent installed on each session host initiates an *outbound* TLS connection to the Azure Virtual Desktop service the moment the VM boots and the agent registers. That connection stays open. When a user connects, their session is relayed to the host over that already-established outbound channel — the session host never has to accept an inbound connection from the internet or even from inside your VNet.

The practical consequence: your session host subnet's NSG needs **outbound** access to the required AVD service endpoints (and to package/patch sources, and anything the user's apps need) — but no inbound rule for RDP is required for the AVD connection itself, and you should not open one. You'll cover the exact required outbound URLs and service tags in the next lesson on AVD networking.

## Host Pools: The Core Compute Object

A **host pool** is a collection of Azure VMs registered as session hosts to the same AVD deployment. Every host pool has a type, set at creation and immutable afterward:

- **Personal**: each user is assigned a specific, dedicated VM (either automatically or by an admin). State persists on that VM between sessions. No load balancing applies — there's nothing to balance, the user always lands on their own machine.
- **Pooled**: many users share a pool of interchangeable, typically non-persistent, multi-session hosts. The broker decides which host a given session lands on using a **load-balancing algorithm**:
    - **Breadth-first** — spreads new sessions across all available hosts to keep per-host load low and performance high. The default and right choice for most knowledge-worker pools.
    - **Depth-first** — fills one host to its `maxSessionLimit` before moving to the next, minimizing the number of running hosts. Pairs naturally with autoscale for cost-sensitive pools where you want to consolidate load onto as few running VMs as possible.

A pooled host pool also sets a **preferred application group type** (Desktop or RemoteApp), which governs default behavior when a user is assigned to both a Desktop and a RemoteApp application group on the same pool — one more reason the pool, not just the app group, is a planning-time decision.

**Validation vs. production**: any host pool — personal or pooled — can be flagged as a **validation environment**. Validation pools receive Azure Virtual Desktop service-side updates and agent changes ahead of production pools, so a small validation pool with a handful of pilot users acts as your canary ring for catching a regression (an agent bug, a broker behavior change) before it reaches the fleet everyone depends on. Plan for at least one validation pool per environment tier you support.

## Application Groups: What Gets Published

An **application group** is a logical container of resources published from a single host pool's session hosts. It comes in two flavors:

- **Desktop application group**: publishes the full desktop. A host pool can have at most one Desktop application group.
- **RemoteApp application group**: publishes one or more individual applications rather than the whole desktop. A host pool can have several RemoteApp application groups, each with a different set of apps assigned to different user groups.

An application group cannot exist independently of a host pool — it's always scoped to exactly one pool — and users are granted access by assigning a Microsoft Entra ID security group (never individual users, as a matter of practice) to the application group.

## Workspaces: What Users See

A **workspace** is the layer users actually experience: it's a logical grouping of one or more application groups, and it's what shows up as a single feed in the Remote Desktop client or web client. Without associating an application group to a workspace, users have access rights but see nothing in their feed — a classic "deployed correctly but nobody can find it" support ticket. A typical design associates several RemoteApp application groups (finance apps, engineering apps) and one Desktop application group into a single workspace per business unit or use case, so the user's feed reflects exactly what they're entitled to, from wherever they sign in.

## Service Limits Worth Planning Around

A few practical constraints shape how you design at scale rather than assume infinite elasticity:

- The Azure **portal's host pool creation wizard** caps a single create operation at 500 session hosts; larger fleets are built by adding hosts in batches through automation (PowerShell, Bicep/ARM, or CLI pipelines) across multiple runs, or by splitting users across multiple host pools sharing one workspace.
- **Availability sets** used for session hosts are capped like any other Azure availability set (200 VMs), which is one more reason large pools lean on availability zones (covered in the BCDR lesson) rather than a single oversized availability set.
- Regional **vCPU quota** is almost always the real bottleneck before any AVD-specific limit — request quota increases early in a rollout, not the week before go-live.
- Each **host pool registration token** used to join new session hosts has an expiration time you set (up to 30 days) — plan your automation to regenerate it rather than treating it as permanent.

## Putting It Together

When you plan an AVD environment, you're really answering four questions in order: which **host pool type** fits the user population (personal for 1:1 persistent desktops, pooled for shared knowledge-worker or task-worker capacity); which **load-balancing algorithm** fits the cost/performance trade-off for a pooled pool; what **application groups** need to be published (one desktop, or a curated set of RemoteApps, or both); and which **workspace** each user's application groups should land in so their feed is coherent. Everything else in this module — networking, images, deployment automation, autoscale, and BCDR — is built on top of the answers to those four questions.

slides.title: Two Layers: Control Plane and Session Hosts
bullets: Microsoft manages the broker, web feed, gateway, diagnostics
You manage the session host VMs, image, network, patching
No control-plane compute shows up in your subscription
This split is where all AVD troubleshooting triage starts
slides.narration: Azure Virtual Desktop has a hard split. Microsoft operates the control plane: the connection broker that matches users to hosts, the web feed, the gateway that relays traffic, and diagnostics, all at global scale, and you never see a VM or a patch cycle for any of it. What you own is the session host layer: the actual Windows virtual machines running in your subscription, your virtual network, built from your image, on your patching schedule. Every troubleshooting conversation later in this course starts by figuring out which side of that line a problem lives on.

slides.title: Reverse Connect: Why No Inbound Ports
bullets: Agent on the session host opens an outbound connection at boot
That connection stays open and relays user sessions
No inbound RDP rule, no public IP required on the host
You only need outbound access to required AVD endpoints
slides.narration: New AVD engineers always ask what inbound firewall rule lets users RDP in. The answer is none. Each session host's agent opens an outbound connection to the Azure Virtual Desktop service the moment it boots and registers, and that connection stays open. When a user connects, their session rides that already-open outbound channel back to the host. You never open an inbound RDP port and you never need a public IP on the session host for this to work. You only need outbound access to the required AVD service endpoints, which we cover in the networking lesson.

slides.title: Host Pools: Personal vs Pooled
bullets: Personal: one dedicated VM per user, state persists
Pooled: many users share interchangeable multi-session hosts
Pooled pools use a load-balancing algorithm to place sessions
Host pool type is set at creation and can't be changed later
slides.narration: Every host pool is either personal or pooled, and that choice is locked in at creation. Personal host pools assign each user their own dedicated virtual machine, so state persists between sessions the way a physical laptop would. Pooled host pools share a set of interchangeable, usually non-persistent, multi-session hosts across many users, and because there's a pool to share, the broker needs a load-balancing algorithm to decide where each new session lands.

slides.title: Breadth-First vs Depth-First
bullets: Breadth-first: spread sessions evenly across all hosts
Depth-first: fill one host to its limit before the next
Breadth-first favors performance per user
Depth-first favors cost consolidation, pairs with autoscale
slides.narration: For pooled host pools you pick one of two algorithms. Breadth-first spreads new sessions evenly across every available host, which keeps per-host load low and protects the user experience — a good default for knowledge workers. Depth-first instead fills one host up to its maximum session limit before moving to the next, which minimizes the number of hosts running at once. Depth-first is the natural partner for autoscale plans that are trying to consolidate load and shut down unused capacity.

slides.title: Application Groups: Desktop and RemoteApp
bullets: An application group publishes resources from one host pool
Desktop type: the full desktop, one per host pool maximum
RemoteApp type: individual apps, multiple per host pool
Access is granted via Entra ID security groups
slides.narration: An application group is a logical container that publishes resources out of exactly one host pool — it can't exist on its own. A Desktop application group publishes the whole desktop, and a host pool can only have one of those. A RemoteApp application group publishes a curated set of individual applications, and a host pool can have several, each assigned to a different group of users. In every case you grant access with a Microsoft Entra ID security group, not individual user assignments.

slides.title: Workspaces: The User's Feed
bullets: A workspace groups one or more application groups
It's what the user actually sees in their client
An unassociated application group is invisible to users
Typical design: group by business unit or use case
slides.narration: A workspace is the layer the user experiences directly: it groups together one or more application groups into a single feed inside the Remote Desktop client or the web client. If you forget to associate an application group with a workspace, the user has access rights on paper but sees nothing when they sign in — a very common early support ticket. A clean design groups related RemoteApp and Desktop application groups into one workspace per business unit or use case.

slides.title: Validation vs Production Host Pools
bullets: Any host pool can be flagged as a validation environment
Validation pools get AVD service updates and agent changes early
A small pilot user group acts as your canary ring
Catch regressions before they hit your production fleet
slides.narration: Any host pool, personal or pooled, can be marked as a validation environment. Validation pools receive Azure Virtual Desktop service updates and agent changes ahead of your production pools. Running a small validation pool with a handful of pilot users gives you a canary ring: if a service update or agent change introduces a regression, you catch it on a handful of test users instead of your entire production fleet.

slides.title: Service Limits to Plan Around
bullets: Portal create-flow caps at 500 session hosts per operation
Availability sets cap at 200 VMs — zones scale further
Regional vCPU quota is usually the real bottleneck
Registration tokens expire — automate their renewal
slides.narration: A handful of practical limits shape design at scale. The Azure portal's host pool creation wizard caps a single operation at 500 session hosts, so large fleets are built in batches through automation. Availability sets cap at 200 virtual machines, which is one reason large pools lean on availability zones instead. Regional vCPU quota is almost always the real constraint, so request increases early. And host pool registration tokens expire on a schedule you set, so your automation needs to handle renewing them, not just the first deployment.

slides.title: Putting It Together
bullets: Pick host pool type for the user population
Pick load-balancing algorithm for cost vs performance
Design application groups for what gets published
Design workspaces for a coherent user feed
slides.narration: Planning an AVD environment comes down to four ordered decisions. Choose the host pool type that fits the user population — personal for one-to-one persistent desktops, pooled for shared capacity. Choose the load-balancing algorithm that fits your cost and performance trade-off. Design the application groups for exactly what needs to be published. And design the workspaces so each user's feed is coherent. Every remaining lesson in this module — networking, images, deployment automation, autoscale, and disaster recovery — builds directly on these four answers.
